## Problem

Assuming the likelihood in (6.3), suppose that $\phi$ is fixed and that we adopt the prior

$$
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2) \propto \frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau^2}.
$$

Show that the resulting posterior

$$
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2\mid\mathbf y)
$$

is improper.

## 1. Marginal likelihood

For the spatial regression model, the marginal likelihood in (6.3) is

$$
\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2,\phi
\sim
N_n\!\left(
X\boldsymbol\beta,
\sigma^2H(\phi)+\tau^2I_n
\right).
$$

Because $\phi$ is fixed, write

$$
H=H(\phi)
$$

and define

$$
\Sigma(\sigma^2,\tau^2)=\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n.
$$

Therefore, the likelihood is

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)
=(2\pi)^{-n/2}|\Sigma(\sigma^2,\tau^2)|^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac12(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)^T
\Sigma(\sigma^2,\tau^2)^{-1}
(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right\}.
$$

## 2. Posterior kernel

Combining the likelihood with the prior gives

$$
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2\mid\mathbf y)
\propto
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)
\frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau^2}.
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2\mid\mathbf y)
\propto{}&
\frac{|\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n|^{-1/2}}
{\sigma^2\tau^2}\\
&\times
\exp\left\{
-\frac12(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)^T
(\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n)^{-1}
(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The posterior is proper only if its normalising constant is finite:

$$
C=
\int_{\mathbb R^p}\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)
\frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau^2}
\,d\sigma^2\,d\tau^2\,d\boldsymbol\beta <\infty.
$$

We will show that $C=\infty$.

## 3. Behaviour as the spatial variance approaches zero

Fix $\tau^2>0$. As $\sigma^2\rightarrow0$,

$$
\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n\longrightarrow\tau^2I_n.
$$

It follows that

$$
|\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n|^{-1/2}
\longrightarrow
|\tau^2I_n|^{-1/2}
=(\tau^2)^{-n/2},
$$

and

$$
(\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n)^{-1}
\longrightarrow
\frac{1}{\tau^2}I_n.
$$

Thus, the likelihood converges to

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,0,\tau^2)
=(2\pi\tau^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2}{2\tau^2}
\right\}.
$$

For every finite $\boldsymbol\beta$ and every $\tau^2>0$, this limiting likelihood is finite and strictly positive. Therefore, near $\sigma^2=0$, the likelihood does not approach zero and cannot cancel the prior factor $1/\sigma^2$.

The posterior consequently behaves like

$$
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2\mid\mathbf y)
\approx
L(\boldsymbol\beta,0,\tau^2)
\frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau^2}.
$$

Its dependence on $\sigma^2$ near zero is therefore proportional to $1/\sigma^2$.

## 4. Rigorous lower-bound argument

Choose a closed and bounded set $B\subset\mathbb R^p$ having positive volume, and choose constants

$$
0<a<b<\infty,
\qquad
\varepsilon>0.
$$

Restrict the parameter space to

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\in B,
\qquad
a\leq\tau^2\leq b,
\qquad
0<\sigma^2\leq\varepsilon.
$$

The likelihood extends continuously to $\sigma^2=0$. Moreover, it is strictly positive on the compact set

$$
B\times[0,\varepsilon]\times[a,b].
$$

Consequently, there is a constant $m>0$ such that

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)\geq m
$$

throughout this set. Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
C
&\geq
\int_B\int_a^b\int_0^\varepsilon
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2)
\frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau^2}
\,d\sigma^2\,d\tau^2\,d\boldsymbol\beta\\
&\geq
m
\int_Bd\boldsymbol\beta
\int_a^b\frac{1}{\tau^2}\,d\tau^2
\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\,d\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $s=\sigma^2$. The last integral is

$$
\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\,d\sigma^2
=
\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{1}{s}\,ds
=\infty.
$$

The other two integrals are finite and strictly positive, so

$$
C=\infty.
$$

Therefore, no finite normalising constant exists.

## 5. The same issue at $\tau^2=0$

There is also a symmetric problem as $\tau^2\rightarrow0$. If $\sigma^2>0$ is fixed and $H$ is positive definite, then

$$
\sigma^2H+\tau^2I_n\longrightarrow\sigma^2H,
$$

so the likelihood again converges to a finite, strictly positive quantity. It therefore cannot cancel the prior factor $1/\tau^2$, and

$$
\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{1}{\tau^2}\,d\tau^2=\infty.
$$

Only one divergent boundary is required to establish impropriety, but here both variance-component boundaries cause the same problem.

## Conclusion

When one variance component approaches zero, the other variance component keeps the covariance matrix nonsingular. The likelihood therefore remains positive at the boundary, while the prior has a non-integrable singularity there. Hence,

$$
\boxed{
p(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2,\tau^2\mid\mathbf y)
\text{ is improper.}
}
$$
